coach_says: The d5 pawn looked free, but your opponent's queen on b3 was guarding it along the b3-c4-d5 diagonal, so Qxd5+ just hands over your queen after Qxd5. The check made it feel forcing, but a check doesn't help if the checking piece can be taken. Before capturing, ask 'who defends this?' and trace every line to the square, especially long diagonals from a queen. A quiet move like Ra6 or Nf5 kept the game level.
concept: pawn was defended by the queen

coach_says: Your f3 knight is pinned to your queen by Bg4, and Black's c6 knight wants to jump to d4 and pile on it. After ...Nd4 and ...Nxf3+, gxf3 wrecks your kingside and ...Bh3 hits your rook. d3 does nothing about that. Play c3 to take d4 away from the knight (or h3 first to ask the bishop) and the pin loses its sting.

This is a known draw: with a c-pawn on the seventh, run your king into the corner with Ka8. Then Qxc7 is stalemate, and if the queen ever stops checking to bring her king closer, you queen the pawn. Kc8 put your king in front of your own pawn and gave Black the free tempo to walk the king over with Ke6, and Qd7 is mate. Remember the bishop-pawn and rook-pawn stalemate tricks against a lone queen.
also: king in front of own pawn

coach_says: Your pawns on a5 and b5 were already rolling at the b3 bishop, so finish the job with ...a4: the bishop has to go back to a2 where it does little, and your knight can then jump to f5 to hit the e3 bishop. Be5 put your bishop on a square the f-pawn can attack, and after f4 White gets time to untangle. When your pawns are chasing a piece, keep pushing before the opponent can reorganise.
also: don't put pieces where pawns can hit them

coach_says: Black has offered the d5 pawn and is attacking e4, so the simplest answer is exd5, which wins a pawn and keeps Black's centre from rolling. After Nc3, Black pushes ...d4 hitting your knight, and it has to go back home to b1 while Black gains space in the centre. Watch out for developing a knight to a square where a pawn can kick it with tempo.

Grabbing c2 sent your bishop deep into White's camp while your f8 bishop and h8 rook are still at home. White answers Bd7+ and Ba4, attacking the c2 bishop, and now Rd8 is checkmate because nothing guards your back rank, so you have to give material back. With your kingside undeveloped, keep the bishop safe with Bg6 and get Bd6 and the rook into play before hunting pawns.
concept: pawn grab with back rank weak

coach_says: White's king is still in the centre and the b4 pawn is only held by a3, so ...a5 at once pries open the queenside: it attacks b4 and opens the a-file for your rook. Bd7 is a useful move but slow, and it lets White play Bd3 to trade off your strong f5 knight. When you're ahead and the enemy king hasn't castled, use pawn levers to open lines right away.
also: open lines while king is in centre

coach_says: After cxd4 your d4 pawn is attacked three times (c6 knight, f5 knight and the queen on b6) and defended only twice (f3 knight and your queen), so Black simply wins it. Bd3 first lets you take off the f5 knight with Bxf5, and then cxd4 is safe. Before recapturing in the centre, count attackers and defenders on the square.

In rook against two bishops, White's h-pawn is the danger: it has no black pawn in front of it and the bishops will escort it. Rh5 attacks h2 and sits in the pawn's path, so it can't run. After c5, White plays h4 and h5 and your rook gets tied up stopping it while your king is far away on the queenside. Stop the passed pawn before making queenside moves.
also: rook in front of the passed pawn

coach_says: You're a pawn down, so look for a way to win it back. Rd2 guards c2 and f2, keeps your e3 bishop's diagonal open to a7, and gets ready for Rd7 hitting f7. Rd4 does attack the bishop, but it just steps to g6, and now your own rook on d4 blocks your bishop from a7. Hitting a piece that can simply move away isn't a gain; aim your pieces at pawns that can't run.
f6 is fine: it asks the e5 knight to leave and is as good as the engine's other choices. Just keep an eye on the e6 bishop and the c6 pawn once the knight jumps in with Nxc6.
Either recapture on d6 is about the same here. cxd6 kept your e5 pawn cramping Black, but exd6 is a reasonable choice and the position was already difficult because of the material.
Kxe7 is right: take the dangerous pawn on e7 straight away before it queens. Your king is now centralised to deal with White's h-pawn.
The position is lost whatever you play: Black's connected queenside pawns and h-pawn are too much for one bishop. Be6 changes nothing meaningful.
Kb3 is as good as anything here; the position is lost with three black pawns against your bishop. Keep looking for stalemate tricks, but there's nothing better.
Bxd3 is the best move: your b5 bishop was attacked by the c3 knight, and trading it for White's good attacking bishop keeps your edge.

Your king on h8 has no escape square, and Rxc5 took a rook off your back rank. White plays Qf7 threatening Qf8+ Rxf8, Rxf8 mate, and while you defend, the e-pawn runs to e6 and e7. Rf8 was the move: it covers your back rank and challenges the f-file. Before grabbing a pawn, check whether the piece doing it is guarding your king.
